screens.title: Implementing OCP: Design Patterns and Abstractions
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we move from the idea of the Open/Closed Principle to concrete ways to implement it. You will learn how to design for change by depending on abstractions—interfaces or abstract classes—so that new behavior can be added without altering existing, tested code. We will apply two behavioral patterns commonly used to achieve this: the Strategy Pattern, for swapping algorithms at runtime, and the Template Method Pattern, for fixing the structure of an algorithm while allowing subclasses to fill in steps. You will also see how Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control let you wire different implementations into a client without the client constructing them itself. For example, a payment processor that used conditional logic can be refactored to depend on a PaymentMethod interface; adding a new payment type then means adding a new implementation, not changing the processor. Throughout the chapter you will read short Java examples that show these refactorings, a hands-on shipping-cost exercise to practice Strategy, and guidance on when not to over-abstract. By the end, you should be able to identify candidate areas for OCP application, pick an appropriate pattern, and refactor a conditional implementation into a clean, extensible design. Consider now: which piece of code in your current project changes most often and would benefit from being open for extension?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Implementing OCP
Implementing OCP: Design Patterns and Abstractions
Turn conditional logic into extension points using interfaces, patterns, and DI.
In this lesson

You will refactor a payment processor to depend on a PaymentMethod interface, learn the Strategy and Template Method patterns, and see how DI/IoC support OCP.

Why it matters

Extensible designs let you add features without touching production code that already works, reducing regressions and speeding delivery.

What you'll practice

Refactoring conditionals, implementing strategy interfaces, creating a Template Method class, and using constructor injection for swapping implementations.

Explore Key Topics
Polymorphism & Abstraction
Depend on interfaces so implementations can be added later without edits.
Strategy Pattern
Encapsulate algorithms and swap them at runtime through a common interface.
DI & IoC
Inject dependencies to avoid clients choosing concrete types, enabling easy replacement.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Terminal demo mode
Payment Refactor
Interface-based processor; add new methods without edits.
Template Method
Fix the algorithm skeleton and let subclasses fill steps.
Dependency Injection
Constructor injection decouples creation from use.
Hands-on Activity
Implement shipping strategies and swap them in a calculator.
Quick start
Start by identifying a conditional block that selects behavior. Ask: who should choose the strategy, and who should only use it? Use constructor injection to provide the chosen strategy at composition time.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives focus on the conceptual skills you need to implement OCP. First, you'll learn how polymorphism and abstraction form the primary mechanisms for extension points: by coding to an interface instead of a concrete class you allow new implementations to be plugged in. For example, a PaymentMethod interface lets different payment implementations be swapped without changing the payment processor. Second, you'll apply the Strategy Pattern to group interchangeable algorithms under a single interface and inject them into a context object, enabling runtime choice of behavior. Third, you'll understand the Template Method Pattern, which fixes the steps of an algorithm in a base class while allowing subclasses to override specific steps; this keeps the algorithm structure stable while permitting extension. Finally, you'll explain how Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control let you supply required implementations from outside, which removes the responsibility of creating dependencies from the client and supports OCP. Each objective links a definition to a practical benefit so you can both reason about designs and refactor existing code safely.

screens.title: Polymorphism and Abstraction as OCP Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism and abstraction are the practical heart of implementing the Open/Closed Principle. Abstraction means defining a contract—an interface or abstract class—that specifies behavior without tying it to a concrete implementation. Polymorphism is the runtime mechanism that lets objects of different classes fulfill that contract and be used interchangeably. Together they create extension points: code depends only on the abstraction, and concrete implementations can be added later. For example, when a PaymentProcessor depends on a PaymentMethod interface, you can add CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, or BankTransferPayment classes without changing the processor. A common beginner misconception is to overuse abstractions: creating interfaces for every class without a real extension need adds complexity. The practical rule is to identify the parts of your system likely to change or to have multiple implementations and apply interfaces there. Concrete example: a logging service might remain a single implementation, while a payment gateway or shipping rate calculator often deserves an interface. To check understanding, try identifying three places in your codebase where behavior changes depending on environment, configuration, or external systems—those are good candidates for abstraction. Key takeaway: abstractions define the stable A P I; polymorphism supplies extensible implementations.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism + Abstraction
keyIdea.text: Depend on contracts, not implementations, so you can add implementations later without modifying clients.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Polymorphism & Abstraction
Polymorphism & Abstraction
Make stable contracts and allow multiple implementations to fulfill them.
Definition
Abstraction defines a contract. Polymorphism lets different classes implement that contract and be used interchangeably.
Analogy
Think of an electric socket as the abstraction; many appliances (implementations) can plug into it without changing the socket.
Common Mistake
Over-abstracting everywhere increases complexity. Only extract interfaces where change or multiple implementations are expected.
Key Takeaway

Abstractions create extension points; polymorphism supplies alternate behavior without editing clients.

Example
A PaymentMethod interface allows many payment implementations. The processor only calls processPayment, unaware of details.
// Define an abstraction
public interface PaymentMethod {
  void processPayment(double amount);
}

// Concrete implementation
public class CreditCardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  @Override
  public void processPayment(double amount) {
    System.out.println("Processing Credit Card payment of $" + amount + " via CreditCardPayment.");
  }
}
Why this helps
Add new payment types without editing the processor; existing tests remain valid.
Misconception check
You still modify code for bug fixes. OCP guides extension for new features, not avoidance of all edits.

screens.title: Refactoring an If-Else Payment Processor
screens.narratorSegment: A common violation of OCP is a processor that chooses behavior with long if-else or switch statements. Those conditionals mean adding a new type requires editing the processor, risking regressions. The clean refactor is to extract an abstraction—a PaymentMethod interface—and let the processor depend on that interface. The chapter gives a compact Java example: define PaymentMethod with processPayment, implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment, and modify the processor to accept a PaymentMethod via its constructor. This change moves the responsibility for payment-specific logic into concrete classes and leaves the processor stable. A practical misconception is thinking this merely moves complexity; instead, the complexity becomes localized and testable. You can unit-test CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment individually and mock PaymentMethod in processor tests. Example walkthrough: write the interface, implement a concrete class, then change the processor to accept PaymentMethod and delegate calls. Add new BankTransferPayment classes later without touching the processor. This approach is the stepping stone to Strategy and to DI frameworks which supply implementations at composition time. After this refactor, adding a payment provider is an additive task, not a risky edit to core logic.

keyIdea.title: Refactor Pattern
keyIdea.text: Replace conditionals with an abstraction and delegate behavior to concrete implementors to achieve OCP.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Refactoring If-Else
Problem: Conditional Dispatcher
Long if-else chains force edits to a central class for every new type.
Steps to refactor:
  1. Extract an interface that declares the operation.
  2. Implement concrete classes for each variant.
  3. Change the dispatcher to accept the interface and delegate the call.
  4. Use DI or composition at wiring time to provide the desired implementation.
Concrete benefit
Processor stays unchanged when adding a new payment; tests for processor remain valid.
Refactor Example (Java)
// 1. Abstraction
public interface PaymentMethod {
  void processPayment(double amount);
}

// 2. Concrete strategies
public class CreditCardPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  @Override
  public void processPayment(double amount) {
    System.out.println("Processing Credit Card payment of $" + amount + " via CreditCardPayment.");
  }
}

public class PayPalPayment implements PaymentMethod {
  @Override
  public void processPayment(double amount) {
    System.out.println("Processing PayPal payment of $" + amount + " via PayPalPayment.");
  }
}

// 3. Processor depends on abstraction
public class OcpPaymentProcessor {
  private PaymentMethod paymentMethod;

  public OcpPaymentProcessor(PaymentMethod paymentMethod) {
    this.paymentMethod = paymentMethod;
  }

  public void executePayment(double amount) {
    paymentMethod.processPayment(amount);
  }
}

screens.title: Strategy Pattern: Roles and Runtime Swaps
screens.narratorSegment: The Strategy Pattern is a canonical way to implement OCP when you have a family of algorithms. The pattern separates three roles: the Strategy interface that defines the operation, ConcreteStrategy classes that implement specific algorithms, and the Context that holds a reference to a Strategy and delegates calls. This separation means the context is closed for modification while the set of strategies is open for extension. A concrete example from the chapter is payments: PaymentMethod is the strategy interface, CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment are concrete strategies, and OcpPaymentProcessor is the context. At runtime you can swap strategies by changing the object passed to the context, or configure the strategy based on runtime data. A subtle misconception is thinking Strategy forces runtime overhead; in most cases the cost is negligible and outweighed by maintainability. Another useful practice is to keep strategy implementations thin and focused on the algorithm so they remain easy to test. Use Strategy for behaviors that change frequently or need multiple implementations depending on environment, configuration, or user choice. The core takeaway: Strategy decouples the algorithm choice from the client that uses it.

keyIdea.title: Strategy Roles
keyIdea.text: Strategy encapsulates algorithms behind an interface; contexts delegate and accept different strategies without change.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Strategy Pattern
Strategy Pattern
Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms and make them swappable at runtime.
When to use
When you need multiple ways to do a task, such as different payment or shipping calculations.
Pro tip
Keep strategies focused; prefer composition over inheritance when implementing algorithms.
Pattern Breakdown
Strategy (Interface)
Defines the algorithm method signature.
ConcreteStrategy
Implements the algorithm in a specific way.
Context
Holds and uses a Strategy reference; delegates calls to it.
Example roles: PaymentMethod is the strategy, CreditCardPayment is a concrete strategy, and OcpPaymentProcessor is the context. Swap strategies at composition time to change behavior without edits.
Concrete Example
Inject a StandardShippingStrategy or ExpressShippingStrategy into a ShippingCostCalculator to obtain different cost results for the same order object.
Misconception
Strategy does not prevent all changes. It prevents changes to the client when adding new algorithms, but tests and some wiring code may need updates.

screens.title: Template Method Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: The Template Method Pattern is another way to keep a class closed to modification while allowing extension. In this pattern, an abstract base class defines the overall algorithm as a final method, and marks some steps as abstract or protected so subclasses supply the specific behavior. The chapter's AbstractReportGenerator demonstrates this: generateAndExportReport is the template method that calls fetchData, formatData, and exportReport. fetchData can be implemented in the base class or left for subclasses, while formatData and exportReport are abstract. If you need a PDF report, create PdfReportGenerator and implement the two abstract steps; if you need CSV, create CsvReportGenerator. The key advantage is that the high-level algorithm—fetch, format, export—stays stable, limiting the places where logic can change. A common misconception is confusing Template Method with Strategy: Template Method relies on inheritance and a fixed sequence, while Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms. Choose Template Method when the sequence is important and only certain steps should vary. For extensibility, keep template methods small and document which steps are extension points so future subclasses follow the intended contract. Template Method Pattern means use a final template method to define algorithm steps and allow subclasses to implement specific steps without changing the skeleton.. In practical terms, fix algorithm structure, allow subclasses to fill steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Template Method
keyIdea.text: Use a final template method to define algorithm steps and allow subclasses to implement specific steps without changing the skeleton.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Template Method
Template Method Pattern
Define the algorithm skeleton in a base class, and let subclasses override specific steps.
Example (Java)
public abstract class AbstractReportGenerator {
  public final void generateAndExportReport() {
    System.out.println("Starting report generation...");
    String data = fetchData();
    String formattedData = formatData(data);
    exportReport(formattedData);
    System.out.println("Report generation complete.");
  }

  protected String fetchData() {
    return "Raw Report Data";
  }

  protected abstract String formatData(String rawData);
  protected abstract void exportReport(String formattedData);
}
Use when
You have a fixed algorithm structure with variable steps, like report generation or parsing pipelines.
Contrast
Unlike Strategy, Template Method uses inheritance and a fixed sequence, useful when order matters.
Concrete Subclasses
PdfReportGenerator and CsvReportGenerator implement formatData and exportReport and reuse the shared skeleton.
Pro tip
Keep template methods concise and document which steps are safe to override to prevent fragile subclasses.
Key Takeaway

Template Method secures algorithm structure while allowing targeted extension via abstract steps.

screens.title: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control are practical patterns that make OCP achievable across an application. IoC is the broader principle: the control of object creation and lifecycle is handed over to a container or composition layer. DI is the technique of supplying an object's dependencies from outside, commonly via constructor or setter injection. When a class receives an IEmailSender in its constructor instead of creating a new SmtpEmailService, the class depends on an abstraction and can accept alternate implementations like AwsSesEmailService. This enables OCP because the consuming class rarely needs modification when swapping implementations. DI also improves testability: in unit tests, inject a mock or stub implementation to exercise behavior deterministically. A common misconception is to think DI requires a framework; you can practice constructor injection manually during refactoring and later adopt a DI container if needed. Practical guidance: prefer constructor injection for required dependencies, keep the composition root near application startup, and avoid service locators hidden inside business logic. These patterns turn prior refactors into maintainable architecture where extensions are composed at wiring time, not by changing consumers.

keyIdea.title: DI and IoC
keyIdea.text: Supply dependencies from outside so clients depend on abstractions; this enables easy swapping and testing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Dependency Injection
Definition
DI: Provide dependencies from outside. IoC: Invert the control of creation and lifecycle to a composition layer or container.
Why it matters
Clients no longer instantiate concrete types, so swapping implementations or mocking in tests is straightforward and safe under OCP principles.
Practical rule
Use constructor injection for required dependencies and keep the wiring at the application composition root.
Example: Constructor Injection
public interface IEmailSender { void send(String to, String subject, String body); }

public class SmtpEmailService implements IEmailSender {
  public void send(String to, String subject, String body) {
    System.out.println("Sending via SMTP to " + to);
  }
}

public class OrderProcessor {
  private final IEmailSender emailSender;

  public OrderProcessor(IEmailSender emailSender) { // dependency injected
    this.emailSender = emailSender;
  }

  public void process(Order order) {
    // ...
    emailSender.send(order.getCustomerEmail(), "Order", "Your order...");
  }
}

// Composition root
IEmailSender sender = new SmtpEmailService();
OrderProcessor processor = new OrderProcessor(sender);

screens.title: Practical Refactoring Workflow for OCP
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring to achieve OCP is easier when you follow a deliberate workflow. First, identify a hotspot: a conditional or switch that changes when new features are added. Second, write tests that capture current behavior so you have a safety net. Third, extract an interface or abstract class that represents the variable behavior. Fourth, implement one or more concrete classes that preserve existing behavior. Fifth, change the client to depend on the abstraction and inject the concrete instance. Finally, add new implementations as needed and extend tests to cover them. A concrete example from this chapter: take the existing payment processor with if-else branches. Add tests for payment flows, extract PaymentMethod, implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment, change the processor to accept PaymentMethod, and run tests. Common misconceptions include skipping tests and assuming small changes will never break behavior; tests are required to ensure you haven't altered semantics. Another pitfall is creating too many tiny interfaces; prefer grouping related operations into a meaningful contract. This stepwise process reduces risk and makes refactoring repeatable across the codebase. Practical Refactoring Workflow for OCP means identify hotspots, add tests, extract abstractions, implement strategies, and inject them to minimize risk.. In practical terms, step-by-step approach to refactor conditionals into extension points. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Checklist

  • Write tests covering current behavior
  • Extract abstraction
  • Implement concrete classes
  • Change client to inject abstraction
  • Run and extend tests

Extracting interfaces before identifying real change drivers can create needless complexity.

Given a payment processor with multiple branches, write tests asserting behavior for each branch. Now adding a BankTransferPayment is an additive task with automated verification.

They lock in current behavior so your refactor does not change semantics accidentally.
Why DI
Injecting implementations at composition keeps refactored clients simple and flexible.

screens.title: Activity: Strategy Pattern for Shipping Cost
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement the Strategy Pattern for shipping cost calculation. You are given an Order class with weight and destination data. The task is to define IShippingStrategy with a calculate method, create three concrete strategies—Standard, Express, International—with the cost formulas specified in the chapter, and implement a ShippingCostCalculator that accepts a strategy via its constructor. The activity exercises the same refactoring pattern: create an abstraction, implement concrete behaviors, and inject the desired strategy. A common misconception is to conflate shipping rules with order logic; instead keep calculation strategies isolated so you can test them independently. When testing, create sample orders and validate each strategy's output. The chapter suggests formulas: Standard = 5.00 + 1.50 per kg, Express = 10.00 + 3.00 per kg, International = 20.00 + 5.00 per kg for non-USA destinations. After you implement the strategies, update main to construct the calculator with each strategy and print results for domestic and international orders. This exercise reinforces the OCP idea: to add a new shipping rule later, implement another strategy and pass it to the calculator—no changes to the calculator required.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.5 › Shipping Strategy Activity
Starter Code (Order)
class Order {
  private double weight; // in kg
  private String destinationCountry;

  public Order(double weight, String destinationCountry) {
    this.weight = weight;
    this.destinationCountry = destinationCountry;
  }

  public double getWeight() { return weight; }
  public String getDestinationCountry() { return destinationCountry; }
}

// In main you will construct orders and a ShippingCostCalculator with different strategies.
Instructions:
  1. Create IShippingStrategy with double calculate(Order order).
  2. Implement StandardShippingStrategy: 5.00 + 1.50 * weight.
  3. Implement ExpressShippingStrategy: 10.00 + 3.00 * weight.
  4. Implement InternationalShippingStrategy: 20.00 + 5.00 * weight if destination is not "USA".
  5. Create ShippingCostCalculator that accepts IShippingStrategy in constructor and delegates calculate.
Example Usage
ShippingCostCalculator calc = new ShippingCostCalculator(new StandardShippingStrategy());
System.out.println("Standard: $" + calc.calculate(domesticOrder));

calc = new ShippingCostCalculator(new ExpressShippingStrategy());
System.out.println("Express: $" + calc.calculate(domesticOrder));

calc = new ShippingCostCalculator(new InternationalShippingStrategy());
System.out.println("International: $" + calc.calculate(internationalOrder));
Key Takeaway

This activity practices extracting a strategy interface, creating concrete strategies, and injecting them into a calculator to satisfy OCP.

screens.title: When OCP Goes Wrong: Over-Abstraction & Misuse
screens.narratorSegment: Applying OCP indiscriminately can create unnecessary complexity. A frequent mistake is extracting interfaces for every single class preemptively. This adds indirection, increases the number of files, and can make code harder to follow. The rule of thumb is to abstract where change is likely—areas that interact with external systems, vary by configuration, or implement business rules that frequently evolve. Another pitfall is using DI to inject too many small services, which fragments responsibilities. Also, confusing OCP with never changing code is a misconception: OCP encourages extension for new features but does not forbid modifying code to fix bugs or improve design. Finally, poorly designed abstractions can lock you into a wrong contract; invest a moment to design a meaningful interface that reflects behavior you expect to remain stable. When in doubt, prefer a pragmatic approach: refactor toward OCP incrementally, backed by tests so you can evolve the abstraction as needs become clearer. In practical terms, avoid creating interfaces for every class or premature abstractions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing Strategies and Mocks with DI
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection simplifies testing by making it easy to provide mock implementations for dependencies. When a class depends on an interface, a unit test can inject a lightweight fake or stub that simulates expected behavior. For example, if OrderProcessor requires an IEmailSender, a test can inject a TestEmailSender that records calls rather than sending real email. This isolates the unit under test and avoids slow or flaky tests involving external systems. DI also improves maintenance: when you change a concrete strategy, tests focused on that strategy will reveal regressions, while client tests remain unchanged if the contract is preserved. A typical misconception is that DI complicates tests because there are more moving parts; in practice, DI reduces coupling and enables clear test boundaries. Best practices: keep tests small, mock only external-side effects, and prefer verifying interactions for collaborators while asserting outputs for pure logic. With DI, you can evolve implementations safely while relying on the stable abstraction contract and test suite. Testing Pattern

Example Test Double
Create a FakeEmailSender that records calls to verify OrderProcessor invoked the email step without sending a real message.
Example (Test Stub)

  boolean sent = false;
  public void send(String to, String subject, String body) { sent = true; }
}

// In test

screens.title: Choosing Between Strategy and Template Method
screens.narratorSegment: Strategy and Template Method both help you adhere to OCP, but they serve different needs. Strategy is the right choice when you have a family of algorithms that you might swap at runtime or compose differently across contexts. It favors composition: the context holds a strategy reference and delegates the algorithm. Template Method is appropriate when the high-level algorithm sequence must stay fixed but some steps vary; it uses inheritance and abstract methods for those steps. A practical guideline: if algorithm order matters and only certain steps vary, prefer Template Method. If you need to switch entire algorithms independently of the context or allow many different combinations, prefer Strategy. Keep in mind that Strategy often leads to easier testing and looser coupling because it relies on composition rather than inheritance. A common misconception is to view them as mutually exclusive; sometimes the two patterns can coexist: the template method might call strategy-like collaborators for particular steps. The core principle is to choose the pattern that minimizes changes to existing, tested code when new behavior is required. Choosing Between Strategy and Template Method means use template method when sequence is fixed; use strategy when algorithms should be interchangeable and composed at runtime.. When to use Strategy

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we move from the idea of the Open/Closed Principle to concrete ways to implement it. You will learn how to design for change by depending on abstractions—interfaces or abstract classes—so that new behavior can be added without altering existing, tested code. We will apply two behavioral patterns commonly used to achieve this: the Strategy Pattern, for swapping algorithms at runtime, and the Template Method Pattern, for fixing the structure of an algorithm while allowing subclasses to fill in steps. You will also see how Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control let you wire different implementations into a client without the client constructing them itself. For example, a payment processor that used conditional logic can be refactored to depend on a PaymentMethod interface; adding a new payment type then means adding a new implementation, not changing the processor. Throughout the chapter you will read short Java examples that show these refactorings, a hands-on shipping-cost exercise to practice Strategy, and guidance on when not to over-abstract. By the end, you should be able to identify candidate areas for OCP application, pick an appropriate pattern, and refactor a conditional implementation into a clean, extensible design. Consider now: which piece of code in your current project changes most often and would benefit from being open for extension?

These objectives focus on the conceptual skills you need to implement OCP. First, you'll learn how polymorphism and abstraction form the primary mechanisms for extension points: by coding to an interface instead of a concrete class you allow new implementations to be plugged in. For example, a PaymentMethod interface lets different payment implementations be swapped without changing the payment processor. Second, you'll apply the Strategy Pattern to group interchangeable algorithms under a single interface and inject them into a context object, enabling runtime choice of behavior. Third, you'll understand the Template Method Pattern, which fixes the steps of an algorithm in a base class while allowing subclasses to override specific steps; this keeps the algorithm structure stable while permitting extension. Finally, you'll explain how Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control let you supply required implementations from outside, which removes the responsibility of creating dependencies from the client and supports OCP. Each objective links a definition to a practical benefit so you can both reason about designs and refactor existing code safely.

This second objectives slide frames how you'll practice and demonstrate the skills. For polymorphism and abstraction, you will refactor a conditional-based payment processor into an interface-based design, creating a PaymentMethod contract and concrete implementations. For Strategy, you will implement multiple shipping strategies and inject them into a ShippingCostCalculator to compare results for domestic and international orders. For Template Method, you will read the AbstractReportGenerator example and outline how to add a new report format without touching the base algorithm. For DI and IoC, you will practice constructor injection and explain why replacing a concrete email sender requires no change to the class that uses it. Each learning objective entwines a measurable task with the conceptual learning: refactor, implement, extend, and inject. These are the actions you'll be assessed on, and they align with the chapter's hands-on activity and suggested quiz questions.

Polymorphism and abstraction are the practical heart of implementing the Open/Closed Principle. Abstraction means defining a contract—an interface or abstract class—that specifies behavior without tying it to a concrete implementation. Polymorphism is the runtime mechanism that lets objects of different classes fulfill that contract and be used interchangeably. Together they create extension points: code depends only on the abstraction, and concrete implementations can be added later. For example, when a PaymentProcessor depends on a PaymentMethod interface, you can add CreditCardPayment, PayPalPayment, or BankTransferPayment classes without changing the processor. A common beginner misconception is to overuse abstractions: creating interfaces for every class without a real extension need adds complexity. The practical rule is to identify the parts of your system likely to change or to have multiple implementations and apply interfaces there. Concrete example: a logging service might remain a single implementation, while a payment gateway or shipping rate calculator often deserves an interface. To check understanding, try identifying three places in your codebase where behavior changes depending on environment, configuration, or external systems—those are good candidates for abstraction. Key takeaway: abstractions define the stable A P I; polymorphism supplies extensible implementations.

A common violation of OCP is a processor that chooses behavior with long if-else or switch statements. Those conditionals mean adding a new type requires editing the processor, risking regressions. The clean refactor is to extract an abstraction—a PaymentMethod interface—and let the processor depend on that interface. The chapter gives a compact Java example: define PaymentMethod with processPayment, implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment, and modify the processor to accept a PaymentMethod via its constructor. This change moves the responsibility for payment-specific logic into concrete classes and leaves the processor stable. A practical misconception is thinking this merely moves complexity; instead, the complexity becomes localized and testable. You can unit-test CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment individually and mock PaymentMethod in processor tests. Example walkthrough: write the interface, implement a concrete class, then change the processor to accept PaymentMethod and delegate calls. Add new BankTransferPayment classes later without touching the processor. This approach is the stepping stone to Strategy and to DI frameworks which supply implementations at composition time. After this refactor, adding a payment provider is an additive task, not a risky edit to core logic.

The Strategy Pattern is a canonical way to implement OCP when you have a family of algorithms. The pattern separates three roles: the Strategy interface that defines the operation, ConcreteStrategy classes that implement specific algorithms, and the Context that holds a reference to a Strategy and delegates calls. This separation means the context is closed for modification while the set of strategies is open for extension. A concrete example from the chapter is payments: PaymentMethod is the strategy interface, CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment are concrete strategies, and OcpPaymentProcessor is the context. At runtime you can swap strategies by changing the object passed to the context, or configure the strategy based on runtime data. A subtle misconception is thinking Strategy forces runtime overhead; in most cases the cost is negligible and outweighed by maintainability. Another useful practice is to keep strategy implementations thin and focused on the algorithm so they remain easy to test. Use Strategy for behaviors that change frequently or need multiple implementations depending on environment, configuration, or user choice. The core takeaway: Strategy decouples the algorithm choice from the client that uses it.

The Template Method Pattern is another way to keep a class closed to modification while allowing extension. In this pattern, an abstract base class defines the overall algorithm as a final method, and marks some steps as abstract or protected so subclasses supply the specific behavior. The chapter's AbstractReportGenerator demonstrates this: generateAndExportReport is the template method that calls fetchData, formatData, and exportReport. fetchData can be implemented in the base class or left for subclasses, while formatData and exportReport are abstract. If you need a PDF report, create PdfReportGenerator and implement the two abstract steps; if you need CSV, create CsvReportGenerator. The key advantage is that the high-level algorithm—fetch, format, export—stays stable, limiting the places where logic can change. A common misconception is confusing Template Method with Strategy: Template Method relies on inheritance and a fixed sequence, while Strategy uses composition to swap entire algorithms. Choose Template Method when the sequence is important and only certain steps should vary. For extensibility, keep template methods small and document which steps are extension points so future subclasses follow the intended contract. Template Method Pattern means use a final template method to define algorithm steps and allow subclasses to implement specific steps without changing the skeleton.. In practical terms, fix algorithm structure, allow subclasses to fill steps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control are practical patterns that make OCP achievable across an application. IoC is the broader principle: the control of object creation and lifecycle is handed over to a container or composition layer. DI is the technique of supplying an object's dependencies from outside, commonly via constructor or setter injection. When a class receives an IEmailSender in its constructor instead of creating a new SmtpEmailService, the class depends on an abstraction and can accept alternate implementations like AwsSesEmailService. This enables OCP because the consuming class rarely needs modification when swapping implementations. DI also improves testability: in unit tests, inject a mock or stub implementation to exercise behavior deterministically. A common misconception is to think DI requires a framework; you can practice constructor injection manually during refactoring and later adopt a DI container if needed. Practical guidance: prefer constructor injection for required dependencies, keep the composition root near application startup, and avoid service locators hidden inside business logic. These patterns turn prior refactors into maintainable architecture where extensions are composed at wiring time, not by changing consumers.

Refactoring to achieve OCP is easier when you follow a deliberate workflow. First, identify a hotspot: a conditional or switch that changes when new features are added. Second, write tests that capture current behavior so you have a safety net. Third, extract an interface or abstract class that represents the variable behavior. Fourth, implement one or more concrete classes that preserve existing behavior. Fifth, change the client to depend on the abstraction and inject the concrete instance. Finally, add new implementations as needed and extend tests to cover them. A concrete example from this chapter: take the existing payment processor with if-else branches. Add tests for payment flows, extract PaymentMethod, implement CreditCardPayment and PayPalPayment, change the processor to accept PaymentMethod, and run tests. Common misconceptions include skipping tests and assuming small changes will never break behavior; tests are required to ensure you haven't altered semantics. Another pitfall is creating too many tiny interfaces; prefer grouping related operations into a meaningful contract. This stepwise process reduces risk and makes refactoring repeatable across the codebase. Practical Refactoring Workflow for OCP means identify hotspots, add tests, extract abstractions, implement strategies, and inject them to minimize risk.. In practical terms, step-by-step approach to refactor conditionals into extension points. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The task is to define IShippingStrategy with a calculate method, create three concrete strategies—Standard, Express, International—with the cost formulas specified in the chapter, and implement a ShippingCostCalculator that accepts a strategy via its constructor. This exercise reinforces the OCP idea: to add a new shipping rule later, implement another strategy and pass it to the calculator—no changes to the calculator required.

This adds indirection, increases the number of files, and can make code harder to follow. The rule of thumb is to abstract where change is likely—areas that interact with external systems, vary by configuration, or implement business rules that frequently evolve. Another pitfall is using DI to inject too many small services, which fragments responsibilities. Also, confusing OCP with never changing code is a misconception: OCP encourages extension for new features but does not forbid modifying code to fix bugs or improve design. Finally, poorly designed abstractions can lock you into a wrong contract; invest a moment to design a meaningful interface that reflects behavior you expect to remain stable. When in doubt, prefer a pragmatic approach: refactor toward OCP incrementally, backed by tests so you can evolve the abstraction as needs become clearer. Dependency Injection simplifies testing by making it easy to provide mock implementations for dependencies. When a class depends on an interface, a unit test can inject a lightweight fake or stub that simulates expected behavior. For example, if OrderProcessor requires an IEmailSender, a test can inject a TestEmailSender that records calls rather than sending real email. This isolates the unit under test and avoids slow or flaky tests involving external systems. DI also improves maintenance: when you change a concrete strategy, tests focused on that strategy will reveal regressions, while client tests remain unchanged if the contract is preserved. A typical misconception is that DI complicates tests because there are more moving parts; in practice, DI reduces coupling and enables clear test boundaries. Best practices: keep tests small, mock only external-side effects, and prefer verifying interactions for collaborators while asserting outputs for pure logic. With DI, you can evolve implementations safely while relying on the stable abstraction contract and test suite. Strategy and Template Method both help you adhere to OCP, but they serve different needs. Strategy is the right choice when you have a family of algorithms that you might swap at runtime or compose differently across contexts. It favors composition: the context holds a strategy reference and delegates the algorithm. Template Method is appropriate when the high-level algorithm sequence must stay fixed but some steps vary; it uses inheritance and abstract methods for those steps. A practical guideline: if algorithm order matters and only certain steps vary, prefer Template Method. If you need to switch entire algorithms independently of the context or allow many different combinations, prefer Strategy. Keep in mind that Strategy often leads to easier testing and looser coupling because it relies on composition rather than inheritance. A common misconception is to view them as mutually exclusive; sometimes the two patterns can coexist: the template method might call strategy-like collaborators for particular steps. The core principle is to choose the pattern that minimizes changes to existing, tested code when new behavior is required. Let's recap important terms. Polymorphism is the ability for objects of different classes to be treated as a common type, enabling interchangeable implementations. Abstraction refers to defining contracts—interfaces or abstract classes—that hide implementation details and expose only required behavior. The Strategy Pattern defines a family of algorithms behind an interface so they can be swapped without changing the context. These concepts are the building blocks of OCP: abstractions provide stable points, polymorphism supplies extension, and Strategy is a repeatable pattern to encapsulate variable behavior. Remember these definitions and think about how they map to the code you've seen: identify interfaces, find polymorphic call sites, and use Strategy to separate algorithms. Finish by remembering three enablers for maintainable, open-for-extension systems. The Template Method Pattern secures algorithm structure while allowing subclasses to customize steps. Dependency Injection is the technique of supplying dependencies from outside so clients remain ignorant of concrete implementations. Inversion of Control is the broader principle that moves responsibility for object creation and lifecycle out of business logic and into a composition root or container. Together, DI and IoC make it practical to wire new implementations into a running system without changing the consumers, and Template Method and Strategy offer clear patterns for where to apply those abstractions.
